title: A bytecode interpreter

milestone.title: From Machine Code to Modern Languages

description:
Python runs its bytecode on a **stack machine**: instructions push values onto a stack and pop them off to work on them. Write a tiny one:

```python
def run(program)    # program is a list of instructions; returns a list of everything PRINT printed
```

Each instruction is a tuple:

| Instruction | Does |
|---|---|
| `("PUSH", n)` | push the number n |
| `("ADD",)` | pop two values, push their sum |
| `("SUB",)` | pop b, then pop a, push a − b |
| `("MUL",)` | pop two values, push their product |
| `("DUP",)` | push another copy of the top value |
| `("PRINT",)` | pop a value and add it to the output |
| `("JUMPZ", i)` | pop a value; if it is 0, continue at instruction number i |
| `("JUMP", i)` | continue at instruction number i |

`(2 + 3) * 4` is `PUSH 2, PUSH 3, ADD, PUSH 4, MUL, PRINT`, which prints 20.

A Python list is a stack: `stack.append(x)` pushes, `stack.pop()` pops. Keep a program counter `pc` like the CPU of 4.04 and stop when it runs past the last instruction.

starter.solution.py:
def run(program):
    stack = []
    output = []
    return output

hints: Keep a `stack` list and a program counter `pc`. Each step reads `program[pc]`, moves `pc` on, and does what the operation says.
For `SUB`, pop `b` first and then `a`, and push `a - b`: the order matters. Jumps set `pc` instead of letting it move on.
